Explain how env_prefix affects lookup, what happens when no value exists, the accepted string forms and errors for boolean casting, how None and other casts are handled, and whether a value read through Environ can later be set or deleted through that wrapper. Assume any supplied cast is a named function or type with a __name__ attribute.
case_results.answer:
`Config.get` first prefixes the requested key with `env_prefix`, then checks the supplied environment mapping, the parsed env-file values, and finally the default—in that order. The prefix applies to all three lookups; if none contains the prefixed key and no default was supplied, it raises `KeyError` naming that key. ( `starlette/config.py`, `Config.get`.)

For `cast=bool` and a string value, matching is case-insensitive and accepts only `"true"` or `"1"` as true, and `"false"` or `"0"` as false. Any other string raises `ValueError` saying the value is not a valid bool. If the value is `None`, or no cast is supplied, it is returned unchanged. Otherwise Config calls `cast(value)`; a `TypeError` or `ValueError` from that call is re-raised as a `ValueError` identifying the cast by its `__name__`. (`starlette/config.py`, `Config._perform_cast`.)

The `Environ` wrapper tracks keys read through `__getitem__`. A tracked key cannot subsequently be set or deleted through the wrapper: either operation raises `EnvironError`. Keys not yet read can be set or deleted normally. (`starlette/config.py`, `Environ.__getitem__`, `Environ.__setitem__`, `Environ.__delitem__`.)

case_results.question: When decoding response text, how does HTTPX choose between an explicitly assigned encoding, the Content-Type charset, and default_encoding? Describe handling of an unrecognized header charset when the body is already buffered, when a callable default is invoked, and what happens if encoding is first inspected before an unbuffered body is read with no charset header and a callable default. Also explain text caching and whether encoding can be reassigned after text has been accessed.
case_results.answer: I can’t reliably describe HTTPX’s response-text decoding behavior from the retrieved code. The available excerpts from `httpx/_models.py` show `_is_known_encoding()` (lines 56–64) and `_parse_content_type_charset()` (lines 85–90), but not the `Response` implementation that chooses an encoding, buffers or decodes the body, caches text, or handles reassignment. So I could not determine the requested cases: an unrecognized header charset with a buffered body, invocation of a callable `default_encoding`, first inspecting encoding before reading an unbuffered body without a charset, or whether encoding can be reassigned after accessing text.

case_results.question: When can a URL be excluded from environment proxies by a no-proxy rule? Explain explicit no_proxy versus lowercase and uppercase environment variables, hostname-less URLs, and how comma-separated rules match IPv4 addresses/subnets versus hostnames with optional ports. Include subnet-prefix validity, what happens when no rule matches, how native bypass-check errors and temporarily changed environment values are handled, and what environment-proxy lookup returns for a bypassed URL.
case_results.answer:
A URL is excluded from environment proxies whenever `should_bypass_proxies` returns true (`src/requests/utils.py:765–823`). An explicit `no_proxy` argument takes precedence; only when it is `None` does the function consult the environment, preferring lowercase `no_proxy` and falling back to uppercase `NO_PROXY` (`src/requests/utils.py:772–782`). A URL with no hostname—such as `file:///`—is always treated as bypassed (`src/requests/utils.py:784–786`).

The selected comma-separated list is stripped of spaces and empty entries. For an IPv4 URL, a rule can match the exact address or a valid CIDR subnet; for other hostnames, a rule matches as a suffix of the hostname, or of the hostname plus its port when the URL has one (`src/requests/utils.py:788–811`). CIDR syntax must contain exactly one slash, a numeric prefix from 1 through 32, and a valid IPv4 address before the slash (`src/requests/utils.py:719–740`). If no list rule matches, the code asks the platform’s `proxy_bypass`; `TypeError` and `socket.gaierror` from that check are treated as “do not bypass” (`src/requests/utils.py:813–823`). During the native check, an explicit `no_proxy` value is temporarily set in the environment and the previous value is restored afterward; if it was originally unset, the temporary variable is removed (`src/requests/utils.py:743–762, 813–818`). Finally, `get_environ_proxies` returns an empty dictionary for a bypassed URL, and otherwise returns the environment proxy mapping (`src/requests/utils.py:826–835`).

case_results.question: How does Config resolve and cast a setting when an environment mapping, an env file, and a default may all provide values? Explain how env_prefix affects lookup, what happens when no value exists, the accepted string forms and errors for boolean casting, how None and other casts are handled, and whether a value read through Environ can later be set or deleted through that wrapper. Assume any supplied cast is a named function or type with a __name__ attribute.
case_results.answer:
`Config.get()` prefixes the requested name first (`env_prefix + key`); that fully prefixed key is used for environment lookup, env-file lookup, casting, and any error message (`starlette/config.py:92–107`). The lookup order is the supplied environment mapping first, then values loaded from the env file, then the default. The first value found is cast and returned; a default is also passed through the cast. If none exists and no default was supplied, it raises `KeyError` naming the prefixed key (`starlette/config.py:98–107`).

With `cast=bool` and a string value, casting is case-insensitive and accepts only `"true"` or `"1"` as true, and `"false"` or `"0"` as false; any other string raises `ValueError` stating it is not a valid bool (`starlette/config.py:129–134`). If `cast` is `None`, or the value is `None`, the value is returned unchanged. Otherwise, `cast(value)` is called; a `TypeError` or `ValueError` from that call is re-raised as a `ValueError` saying the value is not a valid `cast.__name__` (`starlette/config.py:121–138`).

`Environ` tracks keys read through its `__getitem__`; afterward, setting or deleting that key through the wrapper raises `EnvironError`. Reads that fail still mark the key as read, because tracking occurs before the underlying lookup (`starlette/config.py:17–34`).

case_results.question: When PreparedRequest.copy invokes _copy_cookie_jar, what happens for no jar, a jar exposing copy(), and a generic CookieJar without copy()? For a RequestsCookieJar, explain whether the returned jar, its cookie objects, and its policy are shared with the original, including the depth of copying. Would assigning a different value attribute to a copied cookie or mutating the policy through the copied jar affect the original?
case_results.answer:
`PreparedRequest.copy()` assigns `_cookies` from `_copy_cookie_jar(self._cookies)` (`src/requests/models.py`, `PreparedRequest.copy`). If the jar is `None`, the helper returns `None`; if it has a `copy()` method, the helper returns `jar.copy()`; otherwise it shallow-copies the jar, clears that new jar, and inserts a shallow copy of each cookie (`src/requests/cookies.py:440–452`).

For a `RequestsCookieJar`, `copy()` creates a new jar, sets its policy to the original jar’s policy, then updates it with the original cookies (`src/requests/cookies.py:428–437`). Its `update()` shallow-copies each cookie (`src/requests/cookies.py:358–364`). Thus the returned jar and cookie objects are distinct, but the policy object is shared; this is a shallow, not deep, copy. Assigning a new `value` to a copied cookie won’t change the original cookie’s value, but mutating the shared policy through the copied jar can affect the original as well.

case_results.question: An existing hook caller has implementations but no specification. Once a matching specification is recognized during a later specification addition, how is it attached, and what happens if an existing implementation declares a required positional parameter absent from the specification's required positional parameters? Explain whether the failed addition leaves the caller unspecified, whether retrying with a corrected specification can replace it, and what happens when a supplied namespace contains no matching specifications.
case_results.answer:
When `add_hookspecs` finds a matching hook caller that already has implementations, it calls `hc.set_specification(module_or_class, spec_opts)` and then validates each implementation with `_verify_hook` (`src/pluggy/_manager.py`, `PluginManager.add_hookspecs`). `set_specification` rejects a caller that already has a spec; otherwise it constructs and assigns a `HookSpec` (`src/pluggy/_hooks.py`, `HookCaller.set_specification`).

Validation compares an implementation’s argument names with the specification’s argument names. If the implementation declares an argument absent from the spec, `_verify_hook` raises `PluginValidationError` (`src/pluggy/_manager.py`, `PluginManager._verify_hook`). The assignment happens before validation, so the failed addition does **not** leave that caller unspecified: its spec has already been set. A corrected retry therefore cannot replace that spec through this path; `set_specification` raises `ValueError` because a spec is already registered. If the supplied namespace contains no recognized hookspecs, `add_hookspecs` raises `ValueError` (“did not find any … hooks”) (`src/pluggy/_manager.py`, `PluginManager.add_hookspecs`).

I could not determine from the returned source whether a namespace containing some matching specs but none for this particular caller has any further effect on that caller.

case_results.question: On non-Windows platforms, how does Click's standard output helper handle ANSI styling for text when its color setting is explicit, inherited from an active context, or unspecified? Contrast this with nonempty bytes sent to a text stream with a binary buffer, including flush order, the fallback if no binary writer is found, and a call with no message and newline disabled.
case_results.answer:
On non-Windows platforms, `click.echo` resolves `color` only for text output: an explicit `True` or `False` is used as-is; if it is `None`, Click inherits the active context’s `color`, or remains `None` if there is no active context (`src/click/globals.py`, `resolve_color_default`; `src/click/utils.py:298–315`). It then strips ANSI codes when `should_strip_ansi(file, color)` says to do so; otherwise the text is left styled (`src/click/utils.py:306–315`).

Nonempty `bytes` or `bytearray` take a separate path: if Click finds a binary writer, it flushes the text stream first, writes the bytes to the binary stream, flushes that stream, and returns (`src/click/utils.py:294–304`). This bypasses the ANSI-style handling. If no binary writer is found, Click falls through to writing the bytes to the supplied text stream and flushing it (`src/click/utils.py:300–301, 318–320`). Finally, with no message and `nl=False`, `out` is empty, so Click just flushes the stream and returns, without color handling or a write (`src/click/utils.py:285–289`).

case_results.question: When retrieving typed extra attributes from an AnyIO file stream, how are the underlying file object, path, and file number made available? Explain the exact conditions for including the optional attributes, whether their values are captured or obtained through getters, what happens for an absent attribute with and without a supplied default, and whether that default also hides failures while constructing the attribute mapping or invoking a getter.
case_results.answer:
`FileReadStream` and `FileWriteStream` inherit `_BaseFileStream.extra_attributes`, which returns a mapping from typed attribute keys to zero-argument getters (`src/anyio/streams/file.py:27-58`).

- The underlying file is always included as `FileStreamAttribute.file`; its getter returns `self._file`.
- The path is included only when `hasattr(self._file, "name")` is true. Its getter constructs `Path(self._file.name)` when called.
- The file number is included only if calling `self._file.fileno()` while building the mapping does **not** raise `UnsupportedOperation`. The mapping stores a getter that calls `fileno()` again when the value is retrieved. Other failures during that initial call are not caught.

These values are therefore generally obtained through getters rather than captured in the mapping; `fileno()` is additionally probed once during mapping construction to decide whether to include its getter. `TypedAttributeProvider.extra()` catches a missing key: without a supplied default it raises `TypedAttributeLookupError`, and with a default it returns that default (`src/anyio/_core/_typedattr.py:59-81`). But the default applies only to a missing mapping key: mapping-construction errors or exceptions raised by an included getter are not caught by that fallback.

case_results.question: For TagTracer, how do nested subtracers build their tags and how does processor selection treat a colon-separated registration versus a parent-tag registration? Explain how an installed writer renders ordinary arguments and a trailing dictionary at a nonzero indent, whether processors receive that rendered form or the original arguments, and what happens for an emission with no arguments or with no writer.
case_results.answer:
A root tracer created with `get("parent")` starts with the tag tuple `("parent",)`; each nested subtracer’s `get("child")` appends a component, producing `("parent", "child")` rather than replacing the parent tag (`src/pluggy/_tracing.py`, lines 23–24 and 64–73). Processor registration with a colon-separated string splits it into that same tuple form, while tuple registration is used as given; dispatch looks up the exact full tag tuple, so registering `parent:child` matches the nested tracer, but registering only `parent` does not act as a fallback for it (lines 47–51 and 56–61).

With a writer installed, an emission with arguments is formatted at the current indent: ordinary arguments are converted to strings and joined with spaces, then the colon-joined tags are shown in brackets; if the final argument is a dictionary, it is omitted from that joined content and its entries are rendered on following indented lines (lines 26–41, 43–45). At a nonzero indent, the content line gets two spaces per indent level, and each dictionary entry gets four additional spaces (lines 33–40). The processor receives the original tag tuple and argument tuple, including any trailing dictionary—not the rendered string sent to the writer (lines 43–51). If there are no arguments, the writer is not called; processor dispatch is still attempted. If there is no writer, no message is rendered, but processor dispatch is likewise still attempted (lines 43–51).

case_results.question: When retrieving typed extra attributes from an AnyIO file stream, how are the underlying file object, path, and file number made available? Explain the exact conditions for including the optional attributes, whether their values are captured or obtained through getters, what happens for an absent attribute with and without a supplied default, and whether that default also hides failures while constructing the attribute mapping or invoking a getter.
case_results.answer:
In `src/anyio/streams/file.py`, `FileStreamAttribute.file` is always included in the stream’s `extra_attributes` mapping, with a getter that returns the underlying file object (`lambda: self._file`; lines 43–46). The optional `path` entry is included only when `hasattr(self._file, "name")` is true; its getter constructs and returns `Path(self._file.name)` when called (lines 48–49). The optional `fileno` entry is included only if calling `self._file.fileno()` while building the mapping does **not** raise `UnsupportedOperation`; its getter calls `fileno()` again, so the number is obtained on retrieval rather than captured during mapping construction (lines 51–56).

`TypedAttributeProvider.extra()` looks up the requested key in `extra_attributes`; if it is absent, it raises `TypedAttributeLookupError` when no default was supplied, or returns the supplied default otherwise (`src/anyio/_core/_typedattr.py`, lines 73–80). The default applies only to a missing key: it does not catch failures while evaluating `extra_attributes`, nor exceptions raised by the selected getter, which is invoked after the lookup’s `try` block. Thus, for example, a `fileno()` error other than `UnsupportedOperation` during mapping construction—or an error from the getter on retrieval—is not hidden by a default.

case_results.question: For an option configured to prompt, how do command-line values, environment values, context default-map values, and the option default affect whether prompting happens? Explain the required/prompt_required and resilient-parsing gates, the source recorded after a prompt, and how boolean confirmation differs from ordinary value prompting, including evaluation of callable defaults and input-processing settings.
case_results.answer:
`consume_value` first obtains a value in precedence order: command line, environment, context default map, then the option default (`typer/_click/core.py`, `consume_value`). The prompt gate in `Option.consume_value` only prompts when the recorded source is `None` or `DEFAULT`, prompting is configured, either `required` or `prompt_required` is true, and `ctx.resilient_parsing` is false (`typer/core.py`, `Option.consume_value`). Thus command-line, environment, and default-map values suppress prompting; an option default does not suppress it, though it is passed as the prompt’s default. After prompting, the source is recorded as `ParameterSource.PROMPT` (`typer/core.py`, `Option.consume_value`).

`prompt_for_value` evaluates `self.get_default(ctx)` before interacting, so callable defaults are evaluated at that point; boolean flags instead use a yes/no confirmation, coercing any non-`None` default to `bool` (`typer/core.py`, `prompt_for_value`). Ordinary prompts pass the default, option type, `hide_input`, `show_choices`, `confirmation_prompt`, and a `value_proc` that calls `process_value`; boolean confirmation does not use those ordinary value-prompt arguments (`typer/core.py`, `prompt_for_value`). The returned code does not establish the precise behavior of callable defaults (for example, whether/how they are invoked) or all input-processing settings beyond showing that `process_value` is used for ordinary prompts.

case_results.question: A task is waiting on an AnyIO condition and may be cancelled before or just after another task notifies it. Explain the ownership check and queue/lock transitions on entering the wait, how notifying a limited number differs from notifying all waiters, how an interrupted wait removes or passes on its notification, and what lock state is restored before the wait finishes or propagates an error.
case_results.answer:
`Condition.wait()` first checkpoints for cancellation, then verifies that the current task owns the underlying lock; otherwise it raises `RuntimeError` before changing the waiter queue or releasing the lock (`src/anyio/_core/_synchronization.py`, lines 335–341; ownership check at 289–291). It appends a new `Event` to the FIFO waiter deque, releases the lock, and waits on that event (lines 339–343).

`notify(n)` also requires the caller to own the lock, then removes up to `n` events from the *front* of the queue and sets them; it stops if the queue is empty (lines 316–325). `notify_all()` sets every queued event and clears the queue (lines 327–333).

If a wait is interrupted, the handler checks whether its event was set: if not, it removes that event from the queue; if it was set but other waiters remain, it sets the next queued event so the notification is passed on (lines 344–351). In either the normal or exceptional path, the `finally` block reacquires the lock inside a shielded cancel scope before the wait completes or propagates the error (lines 353–355).

case_results.question: How does resolve_types use globalns, localns, and include_extras to resolve field types, and how do its normal field lookup and explicit attribs path differ? Explain which field metadata is changed and what is returned, why repeat calls and subclass calls behave differently, and what happens to errors and the resolved marker if type-hint resolution fails.
case_results.answer:
`resolve_types(cls, globalns=None, localns=None, attribs=None, include_extras=True)` passes `globalns` and `localns` to `typing.get_type_hints`; absent overrides, the names are looked up in the class’s defining module. On Python 3.9+, it also passes `include_extras` (default `True`), which preserves extra annotation information where supported. [src/attr/_funcs.py:451–465, 507–512]

After resolving hints, the normal path (`attribs is None`) iterates `fields(cls)`; the explicit `attribs` path iterates only the supplied list instead. In either path, it updates a field only when its `name` is present in the hints, replacing the frozen field’s `type` via `_OBJ_SETATTR`; other field metadata is not changed. [src/attr/_funcs.py:513–516]

The function marks success by assigning `cls.__attrs_types_resolved__ = cls`, then returns `cls` (so it can be used as a decorator). A repeat call on that same class skips resolution because the marker equals the class; a subclass does not inherit a marker equal to itself, so it can still be resolved. [src/attr/_funcs.py:502–505, 517–522]

If `typing.get_type_hints` fails, the exception propagates (the docs specifically identify `NameError` for unresolved names). Since the marker assignment happens only after hint resolution and field updates, a failure there does not mark the class resolved; subsequent calls will try again. [src/attr/_funcs.py:491–492, 512–519]

case_results.question: When retrieving typed extra attributes from an AnyIO file stream, how are the underlying file object, path, and file number made available? Explain the exact conditions for including the optional attributes, whether their values are captured or obtained through getters, what happens for an absent attribute with and without a supplied default, and whether that default also hides failures while constructing the attribute mapping or invoking a getter.
case_results.answer:
`FileStreamAttribute` defines the typed keys `file`, `path`, and `fileno` in `src/anyio/streams/file.py` (lines 26–32). A file stream always includes `file`, whose getter returns the underlying `self._file`. It includes `path` only when `hasattr(self._file, "name")` is true; that getter constructs a `Path` from the file’s `name`. It includes `fileno` only if calling `self._file.fileno()` while building the mapping does not raise `UnsupportedOperation`; its getter calls `fileno()` again. Thus the mapping stores getters, not captured values (`src/anyio/streams/file.py`, lines 43–58).

When `extra()` finds no getter for a key, it raises `TypedAttributeLookupError` if no default was supplied, or returns the supplied default otherwise (`src/anyio/_core/_typedattr.py`, lines 61–81). That fallback applies only to a missing mapping key: it does not suppress errors raised while constructing the file stream’s `extra_attributes` mapping or while invoking a getter for a present key. In particular, the `fileno()` probe suppresses only `UnsupportedOperation`; other probe errors propagate, as do errors from later getter calls.

case_results.question: Why does the default filter preserve an ordinary false value unless its boolean option is enabled, yet accept even a StrictUndefined value without truth-testing it? Also explain why missing.child['leaf']|default('fallback') can reach the fallback with ChainableUndefined but fail with ordinary Undefined, and whether ChainableUndefined also makes arithmetic on a missing value safe before the filter runs.
case_results.answer:
`do_default` checks `isinstance(value, Undefined)` first, and only evaluates `not value` when the `boolean` option is true (`src/jinja2/filters.py:546–576`). So an ordinary false value is preserved by default, while `default(..., true)` also substitutes falsey values. The `Undefined` type check itself does not truth-test the value, which is why the filter can accept a `StrictUndefined` without triggering its error-raising `__bool__` (`src/jinja2/runtime.py:1039–1062`).

With `ChainableUndefined`, missing attribute and item accesses return the same undefined object, allowing `missing.child['leaf']` to reach the filter; the filter then recognizes it as `Undefined` and returns the fallback (`src/jinja2/runtime.py:970–1005`; `src/jinja2/filters.py:573–576`). Ordinary `Undefined` raises on those accesses, so the chain fails before `default` is applied (`src/jinja2/runtime.py:862–880`). Chainability does **not** make arithmetic safe: it only overrides attribute and item access, while inherited arithmetic operators still raise, so arithmetic on a missing value fails before a later filter can run (`src/jinja2/runtime.py:872–880`, `970–1005`).

case_results.question: When a template serializes a value with the tojson filter, how are the serializer and its keyword arguments selected by default and by policy overrides? Explain how a per-call indent interacts with those policy arguments, which extra HTML-safety transformations and result type are applied, and why the result still needs care inside a double-quoted HTML attribute.
case_results.answer:
`do_tojson` in `src/jinja2/filters.py` takes its serializer and keyword arguments from the environment policies `json.dumps_function` and `json.dumps_kwargs`. By default, `src/jinja2/defaults.py` sets the serializer policy to `None` and kwargs to `{"sort_keys": True}`; `htmlsafe_json_dumps` in `src/jinja2/utils.py` resolves a `None` serializer to `json.dumps`.

A per-call `indent` is added to the policy kwargs only when supplied. In that case, `do_tojson` copies the kwargs first, so it does not mutate the policy dictionary; the per-call `indent` value replaces any policy `indent`. The resulting JSON has `<`, `>`, `&`, and `'` replaced with Unicode escapes, then is wrapped as `Markup`, so it is marked safe for HTML and script-tag rendering (`src/jinja2/utils.py`, `htmlsafe_json_dumps`).

The documented exception is a double-quoted HTML attribute: the result is not safe there, so use single quotes around the attribute or apply `|forceescape` (`src/jinja2/filters.py`, `do_tojson`; `src/jinja2/utils.py`, `htmlsafe_json_dumps`). I could not determine from the returned code why those transformations alone do not make double-quoted attributes safe.

case_results.question: How does Starlette handle a CORS preflight request without invoking the downstream application? Explain which requests qualify, how allowed origins, methods, and requested headers are checked (including wildcards and origin regexes), how allow_credentials changes the returned origin and Vary behavior when all origins are allowed, and what status/body are returned when checks pass or multiple checks fail.
case_results.answer:
`CORSMiddleware` intercepts a preflight when the request is HTTP, has an `Origin` header, and is an `OPTIONS` request containing `Access-Control-Request-Method`. It builds the preflight response itself and returns without calling the downstream app; requests without an origin, and other requests with an origin, follow different paths through the middleware (`starlette/middleware/cors.py`, `CORSMiddleware.__call__`).

The origin is allowed if `allow_origins` contains `"*"`, the origin fully matches `allow_origin_regex`, or it exactly appears in `allow_origins` (`is_allowed_origin`). The requested method must be in `allow_methods`; configuring `"*"` for methods expands it to Starlette’s `ALL_METHODS`. For headers, `"*"` allows the requested headers and echoes their value in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`; otherwise each comma-separated requested header is checked case-insensitively against the configured headers plus the safelisted headers (`__init__`, `preflight_response`).

When all origins are allowed and credentials are **not** enabled, the preflight response uses `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and does not set `Vary: Origin`. With credentials enabled, it instead sets `Vary: Origin` and, for an allowed request, returns that request’s specific origin; it also includes `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (`__init__`, `preflight_response`). A successful preflight returns status **200** with body `OK`. If checks fail, it returns **400** with body `Disallowed CORS ` followed by the failed check names—such as `Disallowed CORS origin, method, headers` when multiple checks fail (`preflight_response`).

case_results.question: How does requires use credentials supplied by AuthenticationMiddleware to authorize HTTP and WebSocket endpoints? Explain what credentials and user are installed when the backend returns None, whether multiple required scopes are all required, and what missing scopes do for synchronous or asynchronous HTTP endpoints with and without a redirect versus WebSocket endpoints. Include the HTTP redirect target/status and whether the protected endpoint executes on denial.
case_results.answer:
`AuthenticationMiddleware` calls the backend for HTTP and WebSocket connections, then installs the returned pair on the scope as `auth` and `user` (`starlette/middleware/authentication.py:28-45`). If the backend returns `None`, it substitutes empty `AuthCredentials()` and an `UnauthenticatedUser()`; the credentials therefore have no scopes (`starlette/authentication.py:105-107`; `starlette/middleware/authentication.py:41-43`).

`requires` checks each requested scope against `conn.auth.scopes` and denies access as soon as any one is missing, so all listed scopes are required (`starlette/authentication.py:23-27, 30-31`). For either synchronous or asynchronous HTTP endpoints, missing scopes produce an `HTTPException` with the configured `status_code` (403 by default) when no redirect is set. With a redirect, it instead returns a `RedirectResponse` with status **303** to the named route, adding the original request URL as the `next` query parameter (`starlette/authentication.py:64-80, 84-99`). In either denial case, the protected endpoint does not execute; it runs only after the scope check passes. For WebSocket endpoints, missing scopes cause the socket to be closed, and the protected endpoint is not called; the decorator does not apply the HTTP redirect or status-code behavior (`starlette/authentication.py:49-61`).

case_results.question: When streaming a template, what changes when output buffering is enabled, and what does the buffer size actually count? Explain the initial and disabled modes, how empty chunks and an incomplete final batch are handled (including an all-empty remainder), whether disabling restarts generation, and what happens for a size of one or less.
case_results.answer:
With buffering disabled by default, a `TemplateStream` yields each string produced by an unbuffered template instruction separately (`src/jinja2/environment.py`, `TemplateStream` docstring, lines 1576–1585). Enabling buffering instead combines items into one string before yielding it; the default requested size is 5 (`enable_buffering`, lines 1655–1661).

The size counts **non-empty strings**, not every generator item: empty strings are added to the buffer but do not advance its count (lines 1636–1647). So a batch can contain more than `size` items if some are empty. At the end of the generator, a non-empty remainder is yielded, including any empty strings buffered alongside it; if the remainder contains only empty strings, it is discarded (lines 1648–1653).

Disabling buffering switches the stream’s next operation back to reading directly from the same underlying generator, so generation continues rather than restarting (lines 1631–1634). A size of 1 or less raises `ValueError("buffer size too small")` (lines 1655–1659).

case_results.question: When completion is installed explicitly for zsh with a supplied program name but no completion-variable name, what variable and script names are chosen? Explain the changes to the user startup file and completion script, including repeated installation, an existing unrelated zstyle customization, and the naming of the generated completion function.
case_results.answer:
For a zsh install, the startup-file changes are handled by `install_zsh` in `typer/_completion_shared.py`: it adds `fpath+=~/.zfunc; autoload -Uz compinit; compinit` to `~/.zshrc` only if that exact line is absent (lines 122–131). It adds `zstyle ':completion:*' menu select` only when the file contains no `zstyle` at all, so an existing unrelated zstyle customization prevents this default from being added (lines 132–138). Repeated installs therefore do not duplicate the setup line or that default style, and the completion script is written to `~/.zfunc/_<program-name>` (lines 140–146).

The generated zsh script uses `#compdef <program-name>` and defines the function `_<program-name-with-hyphens-replaced-by-underscores>_completion`; `get_completion_script` also removes other non-identifier characters from the function name (`typer/_completion_shared.py`, lines 34–42 and 80–93). I could not determine from the returned code what completion-variable name is chosen when the user omits it: the zsh installer and script generator receive `complete_var` as an argument, but the defaulting logic was not shown.

case_results.question: For TagTracer, how do nested subtracers build their tags and how does processor selection treat a colon-separated registration versus a parent-tag registration? Explain how an installed writer renders ordinary arguments and a trailing dictionary at a nonzero indent, whether processors receive that rendered form or the original arguments, and what happens for an emission with no arguments or with no writer.
case_results.answer: Each `TagTracerSub.get(name)` creates a child with the same root and tags formed by appending `name` to its parent’s tag tuple; emitted messages therefore use the full path of tags (joined by `:` in the writer output). Processor lookup is an exact match on that tuple: registering `"a:b"` splits it into `("a", "b")`, so it matches a tracer with those tags, but registering only `"a"` does not also match its child `("a", "b")` (`src/pluggy/_tracing.py`, `TagTracerSub.get`, `TagTracer.setprocessor`, `_processmessage`). With a writer installed, ordinary arguments are stringified and joined with spaces; a trailing dictionary is omitted from that joined text and rendered as indented `name: value` lines. At indent `n`, the main line gets `2n` leading spaces and each dictionary entry gets four additional spaces (`_format_message`). The writer receives this formatted string, while a matching processor receives the original tag and argument tuples—including any trailing dictionary—not the rendered string (`_processmessage`). If an emission has no arguments, the writer is not called; processor lookup still occurs, so a matching processor can still receive the empty argument tuple. Without a writer, no formatted output is produced, but a matching processor can still run.

case_results.question: When HTTPX query parameters contain several values for the same key, how can a caller append a value, replace all values for that key, or remove the key without changing the original parameter object? Explain removal of an absent key, what bracket lookup versus get_list returns, whether editing the returned list mutates the parameters, and what happens if the caller instead tries item assignment or update in place.
case_results.answer:
`QueryParams` is immutable, so use the methods that return a new object and assign the result:

- **Append** a value while preserving existing values: `q = q.add("key", "new")`.
- **Replace all** values for a key: `q = q.set("key", "new")`.
- **Remove** the key and all its values: `q = q.remove("key")`. Removing a key that isn’t present is harmless; it returns a new object unchanged, because removal uses `pop(..., None)`. (All methods: `httpx/_urls.py:536–580`.)

`q["key"]` and `q.get("key")` return only the first value; `q.get_list("key")` returns all values in a new list, so changing that list does not change `q` (`httpx/_urls.py:512–535`; `get_list` copies the stored values at `526–535`). Direct item assignment, such as `q["key"] = "new"`, and `q.update(...)` instead raise `RuntimeError` because `QueryParams` is immutable; the error messages direct callers to `set()` or `merge()` to create an updated copy (`httpx/_urls.py:631–641`).

case_results.question: For wrappers created by cmp_using, what objects do comparison callbacks receive, and what exactly does require_same_type restrict? Explain how a callback returning NotImplemented affects equality and generated inequality, and when missing ordering methods are completed or a missing equality callback causes a construction error.
case_results.answer: `cmp_using` wraps each value in a comparable object with a `.value` attribute; each supplied comparison callback receives the two **unwrapped values** (`self.value`, `other.value`), not the wrapper instances (`src/attr/_cmp.py`, `_make_operator`). With `require_same_type=True`, the wrapper’s comparison methods return `NotImplemented` unless the underlying values have exactly the same type; the check is `other.value.__class__ is self.value.__class__` (`src/attr/_cmp.py`, `_check_same_type`). A callback that itself returns `NotImplemented` is also passed through unchanged. The generated `__ne__` calls `__eq__`, forwards `NotImplemented` if equality returned it, and otherwise returns the negated equality result (`src/attr/_make.py`, `__ne__`). If at least one ordering callback is supplied but fewer than all four (`lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`) are supplied, `functools.total_ordering` completes the ordering methods—but only if `eq` was supplied; otherwise construction raises `ValueError` (`src/attr/_cmp.py`, `cmp_using`).

case_results.question: For an attrs-generated instance representation, how do repr=False and a callable field repr affect displayed fields, and what is displayed for an unset init=False field with ordinary formatting? Explain how a cycle back to the same instance is bounded, whether the recursion guard is shared between threads, and what happens if a custom field formatter raises before representation finishes.
case_results.answer:
The generated `__repr__` omits fields with `repr=False`. A field with a callable `repr` is included, but that callable formats its value instead of ordinary `repr`; fields using ordinary formatting are shown with `!r` (`src/attr/_make.py:1631–1653`). For an included `init=False` field, the generated method uses `getattr(self, name, NOTHING)`, so if the attribute is unset, ordinary formatting displays the `NOTHING` sentinel rather than raising `AttributeError` (`src/attr/_make.py:1644–1651`).

The recursion guard tracks instance IDs: if the same instance is encountered again while it is being represented, its representation is `...` (`src/attr/_make.py:1662–1678`). The tracker is thread-local, so recursion state is shared across nested repr calls in one thread, but not across threads (`src/attr/_compat.py:87–95`). The generated method removes its instance ID in a `finally` block, so the guard is cleaned up even if formatting raises; however, that exception still propagates and the representation does not finish (`src/attr/_make.py:1673–1678`).

case_results.question: When can a URL be excluded from environment proxies by a no-proxy rule? Explain explicit no_proxy versus lowercase and uppercase environment variables, hostname-less URLs, and how comma-separated rules match IPv4 addresses/subnets versus hostnames with optional ports. Include subnet-prefix validity, what happens when no rule matches, how native bypass-check errors and temporarily changed environment values are handled, and what environment-proxy lookup returns for a bypassed URL.
case_results.answer:
In `should_bypass_proxies` (`src/requests/utils.py:765–824`), an explicit `no_proxy` argument takes precedence; only when it is `None` does Requests read the environment. Environment lookup prefers lowercase `no_proxy`, falling back to uppercase `NO_PROXY` (`utils.py:773–783`). A URL with no hostname—such as a `file:///` URL—is bypassed immediately (`utils.py:785–787`).

Rules are split on commas after spaces are removed, and empty entries are ignored (`utils.py:789–791`). For an IPv4 URL, a valid CIDR rule matches addresses in that subnet; a plain IP rule matches only the exact address (`utils.py:793–802`, `utils.py:690–693`). CIDR validity requires one slash, a numeric prefix from **1 through 32**, and an address accepted by `inet_aton`; otherwise it is not treated as a subnet rule (`utils.py:719–740`). For other hostnames, a rule matches when it is a suffix of the hostname, or of the hostname plus its port when the URL has a nonzero port (`utils.py:803–811`).

If no explicit/list rule matches, Requests temporarily sets the lowercase `no_proxy` environment value to the original explicit argument while calling the platform `proxy_bypass`; it restores the previous value afterward, or removes the temporary variable if none existed (`utils.py:748–763`, `800–821`). `TypeError` and `socket.gaierror` from that native check are treated as “not bypassed”; other errors are not caught there (`utils.py:814–818`). If neither mechanism finds a bypass, the function returns `False` (`utils.py:823–824`). `get_environ_proxies` returns an empty dictionary for a bypassed URL, and otherwise returns the environment proxy mapping (`utils.py:832–835`).

case_results.question: In Rich help output, how are hidden entries and missing or empty panel names handled for arguments, options, and subcommands? Describe the panel ordering, whether arguments and options with the same custom panel name share a panel, and whether empty default panels are printed.
case_results.answer: In `typer/rich_utils.py`, `rich_format_help` skips any parameter with `hidden=True` before grouping it, so hidden arguments and options are omitted (lines 591–596). The returned code slice ends as argument panel naming begins, so I can’t determine how missing or empty panel names are handled, whether arguments and options sharing a custom name share a panel, the panel ordering, or whether empty default panels are printed.

case_results.question: A task is waiting on an AnyIO condition and may be cancelled before or just after another task notifies it. Explain the ownership check and queue/lock transitions on entering the wait, how notifying a limited number differs from notifying all waiters, how an interrupted wait removes or passes on its notification, and what lock state is restored before the wait finishes or propagates an error.
case_results.answer:
In `Condition` (`src/anyio/_core/_synchronization.py`), `wait()` first checks for cancellation, then verifies that the current task owns the condition’s underlying lock; otherwise `_check_acquired()` raises `RuntimeError`. It enqueues a fresh event and releases the lock before waiting. `notify(n)` also requires ownership and removes and sets up to `n` events from the front of the queue; `notify_all()` sets every queued event and clears the queue.

If `wait()` is interrupted, it removes its event if it was not notified. If it was already notified but has not resumed, it sets the next queued event so the notification is passed along. In either case, a `finally` block reacquires the lock inside a shielded `CancelScope`, so the lock is restored before the wait returns or propagates the error. **I could not determine from the available code whether lock reacquisition itself can fail, or what lock state callers should expect in that exceptional case.**

case_results.question: For an attrs-generated instance representation, how do repr=False and a callable field repr affect displayed fields, and what is displayed for an unset init=False field with ordinary formatting? Explain how a cycle back to the same instance is bounded, whether the recursion guard is shared between threads, and what happens if a custom field formatter raises before representation finishes.
case_results.answer:
`repr=False` excludes that field from the generated representation; a callable `repr` is used to format the field’s value—for example, a test’s formatter produces `C(a=foo:1)` (`tests/test_dunders.py`, `test_repr` and the callable-formatter test). An unset `init=False` field with ordinary formatting appears as `NOTHING`, as in `C(a=NOTHING)` (`tests/test_dunders.py:407-413`).

When a field refers back to the same instance, the representation emits `...` for the repeated instance, e.g. `Cycle(value=7, cycle=...)` (`tests/test_dunders.py:357-373`). The recursion tracker is a `threading.local()` object, so it is shared across the repr call stack within a thread but is thread-local rather than shared between threads (`src/attr/_compat.py:79-95`). The cited code and tests don’t establish what happens if a custom formatter raises before repr completes, so I can’t say whether or how the guard is cleaned up in that case.

case_results.question: When completion is installed explicitly for zsh with a supplied program name but no completion-variable name, what variable and script names are chosen? Explain the changes to the user startup file and completion script, including repeated installation, an existing unrelated zstyle customization, and the naming of the generated completion function.
case_results.answer:
For a supplied program name `NAME`, with `complete_var` omitted, Typer chooses `_NAME_COMPLETE`: it replaces hyphens with underscores and uppercases the name before adding the `_..._COMPLETE` form (`typer/_completion_shared.py`, `install`). The zsh completion script is written to `~/.zfunc/_NAME` (`install_zsh`); its generated function is `_<sanitized-name>_completion`—hyphens become underscores and other invalid identifier characters are removed (`get_completion_script`, lines 80–93). The script uses that function in its `#compdef`-style completion definition and invokes the program with the chosen completion variable (`COMPLETION_SCRIPT_ZSH`, lines 28–36).

Installation adds `fpath+=~/.zfunc; autoload -Uz compinit; compinit` to `~/.zshrc` only if that exact line is not already present. It adds `zstyle ':completion:*' menu select` only if the startup file contains no `zstyle` at all, so an existing unrelated `zstyle` customization suppresses this addition (`install_zsh`, lines 129–147). Repeated installation therefore avoids duplicating those startup-file lines; it writes the completion script to the same `~/.zfunc/_NAME` path again, replacing its contents (`install_zsh`, lines 129–147).

case_results.question: For TagTracer, how do nested subtracers build their tags and how does processor selection treat a colon-separated registration versus a parent-tag registration? Explain how an installed writer renders ordinary arguments and a trailing dictionary at a nonzero indent, whether processors receive that rendered form or the original arguments, and what happens for an emission with no arguments or with no writer.
case_results.answer:
`TagTracer.get(name)` starts a tracer with the one-element tag tuple `(name,)`; each nested `TagTracerSub.get(name)` appends that name to the existing tuple. The writer joins the tuple with `:` for display, so nested tags render like `parent:child` (`src/pluggy/_tracing.py:23–24, 64–73`).

Processor selection uses an **exact tuple lookup** on the full tag tuple being emitted; it does not fall back to a parent registration (`_tracing.py:43–51`). Registering `"parent:child"` splits on `:` and stores `("parent", "child")`, so it matches that nested emission. Registering `"parent"` stores only `("parent",)`, so it matches an emission from the parent tracer, not one from `parent:child` (`_tracing.py:56–61`).

With a writer installed, ordinary arguments are stringified and joined with spaces; a trailing dictionary is removed from the ordinary arguments and rendered as indented `key: value` lines. At indent level `n`, the message and each dictionary line are prefixed by two spaces times `n`, with dictionary lines getting four additional spaces—for example, at indent 1: `  hello [parent:child]\n    a: 1\n` (`_tracing.py:26–41`; the dictionary formatting is also tested at `testing/test_tracer.py:54–60`). The processor receives the original tag and argument tuples, not that rendered string (`_tracing.py:43–51`). If there are no arguments, the writer is not called; processor lookup still proceeds, so a matching processor can receive the empty argument tuple. If no writer is installed, no rendering occurs, but a matching processor is still called (`_tracing.py:43–51`).

case_results.question: An existing hook caller has implementations but no specification. Once a matching specification is recognized during a later specification addition, how is it attached, and what happens if an existing implementation declares a required positional parameter absent from the specification's required positional parameters? Explain whether the failed addition leaves the caller unspecified, whether retrying with a corrected specification can replace it, and what happens when a supplied namespace contains no matching specifications.
case_results.answer:
In `PluginManager.add_hookspecs` (`src/pluggy/_manager.py`, lines 255–268), when a matching specification is found for an existing `HookCaller`, pluggy calls `hc.set_specification(...)` and then verifies each existing implementation with `_verify_hook`. That verification (`_verify_hook`, lines 340–354) raises `PluginValidationError` if an implementation declares a positional argument absent from the specification’s positional arguments.

The shown code calls `set_specification` **before** validating implementations, so the failed addition does not leave the caller unspecified. It also shows that a later call with a corrected specification would call `set_specification` again, but the code returned does not establish whether that replaces the earlier specification or whether the failed addition’s state is otherwise rolled back. I could not determine what happens when a supplied namespace contains no matching specifications: the code shows that `add_hookspecs` raises `ValueError` if it finds no hooks, but not how that case interacts with existing callers or their implementations.

case_results.question: A session has its default adapters plus custom adapters mounted for "https://api.example.test" and "https://api.example.test/v1/". How does sending a prepared request choose between them, including URL case differences and registration order? Explain whether the shorter host-looking prefix is restricted to that exact host, what remounting an identical prefix does, and what happens when no registered prefix matches.
case_results.answer: `Session.send` selects an adapter for the prepared request’s URL by calling `self.get_adapter(url=request.url)` (`src/requests/sessions.py`, `Session.send`, lines 696–703). The available code search shows that `get_adapter` compares `url.lower().startswith(prefix.lower())`, so URL and prefix case differences do not affect matching (`src/requests/sessions.py`, line 788). The session initializes default `https://` and `http://` adapters, and `mount` is defined in the same file (`src/requests/sessions.py`, lines 446–449, 799). I can’t determine from the returned code how `get_adapter` orders prefixes, whether `mount` reorders entries when an identical prefix is remounted, whether the host-looking prefix is restricted to that host, or what happens when nothing matches; those implementation details weren’t returned.

case_results.question: For a non-redirecting response, how do session response hooks transform what the caller receives? Explain when they run relative to adapter sending, elapsed-time recording, cookie persistence, and non-streamed body consumption; how one callable versus a sequence is invoked and which send options are forwarded; and how return values (including None and a falsey replacement Response) or a raised exception affect subsequent hooks and the final response. If a hook returns a response with history, which responses contribute cookies?
case_results.answer:
For a non-redirecting response, `Session.send` sends through the adapter first, records elapsed time on the adapter’s response, then dispatches response hooks, and only afterward persists cookies (`src/requests/sessions.py`, `Session.send`, lines 702–718). The non-streamed body is consumed later, after redirect handling, at `r.content` when `stream` is false (lines 720–746). Thus hooks run before that body consumption.

In `dispatch_hook` (`src/requests/hooks.py`, lines 22–33), a single callable is wrapped as a one-item sequence; otherwise the configured sequence is iterated. Each hook receives the current response plus the `**kwargs` passed by `Session.send`—the same send options remaining after `allow_redirects` is removed (sessions.py, lines 691–694, 710). A non-`None` return replaces the current response for subsequent hooks; returning `None` leaves it unchanged. A falsey but non-`None` replacement is still adopted. The code does not catch hook exceptions, so a raised exception stops dispatch and propagates rather than yielding a final response.

For cookie persistence, if the final hook-returned response has `history`, `Session.send` extracts cookies from each response in that history, then from the returned response’s `raw` using the original request (sessions.py, lines 712–718). I could not determine from the retrieved code whether those history responses are necessarily the same as the original adapter response or how a hook constructs them.

case_results.question: How does Linux platform-tag generation decide whether musllinux compatibility applies to the running Python rather than merely to the host OS? Explain discovery of the loader and cases that produce no musllinux tags, how its version output is interpreted, the architecture/version ordering of generated tags, and how these tags fit after Linux architecture adjustment and other Linux platform tags.
case_results.answer:
Musllinux tags are based on the **running Python executable**, not simply on the host OS being Linux. In `src/packaging/_musllinux.py`, `_get_musl_version()` reads the executable’s ELF interpreter path, returns no version if the executable cannot be read or parsed, has no interpreter, or its interpreter path does not contain `"musl"`, and otherwise invokes that loader and parses its standard-error output (lines 37–56). `PreparedRequest.copy()` assigns `_copy_cookie_jar(self._cookies)` to the copy’s `_cookies` field (`src/requests/models.py:382–391`). `_copy_cookie_jar` returns `None` when given no jar; if the jar has a `copy()` method, it returns that method’s result; otherwise it shallow-copies the jar, clears the new jar, and inserts a shallow copy of each cookie (`src/requests/cookies.py:440–452`).

For a `RequestsCookieJar`, `copy()` creates a new jar, sets its policy to the original jar’s policy, and updates it from the original (`src/requests/cookies.py:428–437`). The `update()` implementation shallow-copies each cookie (`src/requests/cookies.py:370–375`). So the returned jar and its cookie objects are distinct, but the policy object is shared. Assigning a different `.value` to a copied cookie therefore does not change the original cookie’s value; mutating the shared policy through the copied jar can affect the original’s policy too.

The copies are shallow: the source establishes separate cookie objects and a shared policy, but does not establish whether mutable objects stored inside cookie attributes are themselves copied.

case_results.question: When decoding response text, how does HTTPX choose between an explicitly assigned encoding, the Content-Type charset, and default_encoding? In `Response.encoding` (`httpx/_models.py:653–672`), HTTPX uses this priority: an explicitly assigned encoding, then the `Content-Type` charset, then `default_encoding`. An unknown charset is treated like no usable charset: a string `default_encoding` is used instead; if the default is callable, it is invoked with the buffered body only when `_content` exists. If the body is not buffered yet, that callable is not invoked during encoding lookup, so HTTPX falls back to `"utf-8"` and caches that result in `_encoding`.

`Response.text` (`httpx/_models.py:642–650`) decodes the buffered content using the selected encoding and caches the result in `_text`; an empty body is cached as an empty string. Once text has been accessed, assigning `encoding` raises `ValueError` (`httpx/_models.py:674–686`).

case_results.question: When HTTPX query parameters contain several values for the same key, how can a caller append a value, replace all values for that key, or remove the key without changing the original parameter object? Explain removal of an absent key, what bracket lookup versus get_list returns, whether editing the returned list mutates the parameters, and what happens if the caller instead tries item assignment or update in place.
case_results.answer:
Use the copy-returning methods and rebind the result:

```python
q = q.add("tag", "new")       # appends, preserving existing values
q = q.set("tag", "only")      # replaces all values for "tag" with one
q = q.remove("tag")           # removes the key and all its values
```

Each method returns a new `QueryParams`; the original is unchanged. Removing a key that is absent is harmless: `remove()` uses a default of `None` when popping, so it simply returns a copy with no change. Bracket lookup (`q["tag"]`) returns only the first value, while `q.get_list("tag")` returns all values in a new list—editing that list does not modify `q`. In-place item assignment and `q.update(...)` are not supported: both raise `RuntimeError` because `QueryParams` is immutable; the errors direct callers to `set()` or `merge()` respectively. (See `httpx/_urls.py`, `QueryParams.get_list`, `set`, `add`, `remove`, `merge`, `__getitem__`, `update`, and `__setitem__`.)

case_results.question: How does URLPattern determine which mounted transport a synchronous HTTPX client uses for a URL? Explain the scheme and port constraints, the differences between example.com, *.example.com, and *example.com host patterns, the precedence when several mounts match, and what happens when the winning mount is None or no mount matches.
case_results.answer:
`URLPattern` matches a URL only if each constraint it specifies passes: a nonempty scheme must equal the URL’s scheme, a host pattern must match the URL’s host, and a specified port must equal the URL’s port. Thus, a pattern without a port can match URLs on different ports, while a pattern with a port requires that exact port (`httpx/_utils.py`, `URLPattern.matches`, lines 192–203).

For hosts, `example.com` matches only that exact host; `*.example.com` matches subdomains such as `www.example.com` but not the bare domain; and `*example.com` matches both the bare domain and subdomains (`httpx/_utils.py`, `URLPattern.__init__`, lines 179–190).

Patterns are sorted by priority before lookup: ports take precedence over patterns without ports, then longer hostnames, then longer schemes (`httpx/_utils.py`, `URLPattern.priority`, lines 205–217; `httpx/_client.py`, line 716). The available output confirms that the synchronous client has a `_transport_for_url` method at `httpx/_client.py:760`, but it does not show that method’s body. So I cannot determine from the returned code what it does when the first matching mount has value `None`, or what it does when no mount matches.

case_results.question: How does varnames turn a class, callable instance, or bound method into its pair of parameter-name tuples? Explain which parameter kinds are retained, how defaults divide the tuples, how implicit receiver names are removed, and which introspection failures produce empty tuples rather than propagating.
case_results.answer:
`varnames` in `src/pluggy/_hooks.py:295-357` returns `(args, kwargs)`, a pair of tuples of parameter **names**. For a class, it inspects `__init__`; for a non-routine callable instance, it inspects `__call__` (`:302-311`). It retains only positional-only and positional-or-keyword parameters, in signature order; variadic positional, keyword-only, and variadic keyword parameters are excluded (`:321-330`).

It gathers defaults for those retained parameters and treats the final `len(defaults)` names as `kwargs`; preceding names become `args`. With no defaults, the second tuple is empty (`:331-344`). Despite the tuple’s name, `kwargs` contains parameter names, not the default values. It removes the first parameter when the callable is a bound method, or when the qualified name suggests a method (`"." in qualname`) and that first name is an implicit receiver: `self` normally, or `self`/`obj` on PyPy (`:346-355`).

The function returns empty tuples if a class’s `__init__` is unavailable, retrieving a callable instance’s `__call__` raises, or `inspect.signature` raises `TypeError` (`:302-319`). Other exceptions from signature inspection are not caught there and may propagate.

case_results.question: When can a URL be excluded from environment proxies by a no-proxy rule? Explain explicit no_proxy versus lowercase and uppercase environment variables, hostname-less URLs, and how comma-separated rules match IPv4 addresses/subnets versus hostnames with optional ports. Include subnet-prefix validity, what happens when no rule matches, how native bypass-check errors and temporarily changed environment values are handled, and what environment-proxy lookup returns for a bypassed URL.
case_results.answer:
`should_bypass_proxies` first uses an explicitly supplied `no_proxy`; only when that argument is `None` does it read the environment, preferring lowercase `no_proxy` and falling back to uppercase `NO_PROXY` (`src/requests/utils.py`, `should_bypass_proxies`, lines 772–784). A URL with no hostname (for example, `file:///...`) is bypassed immediately (lines 786–788).

For a hostname, comma-separated rules are stripped of spaces and empty entries ignored. If the hostname is an IPv4 address, valid CIDR rules match addresses in their subnet, while a non-CIDR rule matches only an exactly equal IP. CIDR validity requires one slash, an integer prefix from 1 through 32, and a parseable IPv4 network address; invalid CIDR-like rules are not treated as subnet matches (`src/requests/utils.py`, `is_valid_cidr`, lines 719–740; `should_bypass_proxies`, lines 791–801). For non-IPv4 hostnames, a rule matches when it is a suffix of the hostname, or of `hostname:port` when the URL has a port; matching is suffix-based, not an exact-host-only comparison (lines 802–812).

If no rule matches, Requests temporarily applies the explicit `no_proxy` value to the environment while calling the platform `proxy_bypass`; `TypeError` and `socket.gaierror` from that check are treated as “do not bypass.” The temporary environment change is restored afterward, including deleting the variable if it was originally absent (`src/requests/utils.py`, lines 748–762 and 814–824). If neither rule-based nor native checking indicates a bypass, the URL is not excluded. `get_environ_proxies` returns an empty dictionary for a bypassed URL; otherwise it returns the environment proxies (`src/requests/utils.py`, `get_environ_proxies`, lines 826–835).

case_results.question: On non-Windows platforms, how does Click's standard output helper handle ANSI styling for text when its color setting is explicit, inherited from an active context, or unspecified? Contrast this with nonempty bytes sent to a text stream with a binary buffer, including flush order, the fallback if no binary writer is found, and a call with no message and newline disabled.
case_results.answer:
In `click.utils.echo` (`src/click/utils.py`, lines 219–225 and 305–319), string output resolves the color setting before handling ANSI codes. An explicit `color=True` or `False` is retained; when it is unspecified, `resolve_color_default` (`src/click/globals.py`, lines 55–68) uses the active context’s `ctx.color` if present, otherwise leaves it as `None`. On non-Windows platforms, `echo` then calls `should_strip_ansi(file, color)` and strips ANSI codes when that helper says to; the exact non-Windows decision rule for `None` could not be determined from the returned source.

For nonempty bytes or bytearrays, `echo` instead looks for a binary writer. If it finds one, it flushes the text stream first, writes and flushes the bytes on the binary stream, then returns (`src/click/utils.py`, lines 292–303). If no binary writer is found, it falls through to `file.write(out)` and flushes the text stream (lines 318–319); the exact binary-writer discovery behavior could not be determined from the returned source. With no message and `nl=False`, `out` remains empty, so `echo` flushes the stream and returns without writing anything (lines 281–290).

questions.question: For a coroutine decorated with AnyIO's asynchronous LRU caching utility, assume successful calls, a positive cache size, and no competing-key eviction. How are overlapping calls for the same missing key coordinated, and what does a later unexpired hit do? Explain when a TTL starts and how expiry causes recomputation, how always_checkpoint affects cached hits and the miss lock, and what caching and added-checkpoint behavior changes when maxsize is zero.

criteria.description: A missing key gets a shared placeholder and lock. Under that lock the wrapper rechecks whether a value was supplied by another task; only the task still seeing the placeholder awaits the wrapped function and stores the completed value, while waiting callers reuse that value.

An unexpired completed entry is returned without invoking the wrapped coroutine and is moved to the most-recent end of the ordered cache. Expiration is checked on access with current_time() >= expires_at; an expired entry becomes a missing placeholder with a fresh lock. A new expiry is computed after successful completion as current_time() plus ttl, so ordinary hits do not extend it.

For ordinary completed cache hits, always_checkpoint explicitly adds an awaited checkpoint when true; otherwise this hit path has no await. Missing and expired entries create a lock with fast_acquire set to the inverse of always_checkpoint.

maxsize zero bypasses key construction, lookup, locks and storage entirely and directly awaits the wrapped coroutine each time. This branch adds no explicit checkpoint even if always_checkpoint is true, so any yield on that branch comes from the wrapped call.

material_error_examples: Overlapping callers always run separate copies of the same missing coroutine.
TTL starts when the first caller begins executing the wrapped coroutine.
Every cache hit refreshes the TTL.
always_checkpoint forces an extra checkpoint even in the maxsize=0 branch.

TLS EOF translation and shutdown cleanup
novelty.distinct_mechanism: Asynchronous memoization: same-key in-flight coordination, access-time expiry and cache-hit scheduling. This does not concern executing synchronous work on threads.

questions.question: A task is waiting on an AnyIO condition and may be cancelled before or just after another task notifies it. Explain the ownership check and queue/lock transitions on entering the wait, how notifying a limited number differs from notifying all waiters, how an interrupted wait removes or passes on its notification, and what lock state is restored before the wait finishes or propagates an error.

criteria.description: The condition records the acquiring task when acquisition succeeds, and its ownership check compares that recorded owner with get_current_task(), raising RuntimeError on a mismatch. wait first checks cancellation, then ownership, appends a new Event to the waiter queue and releases the underlying lock before awaiting the event.
notify(n) checks ownership, pops from the left and sets up to n queued events, stopping if the queue is empty. notify_all also checks ownership, sets all queued events and clears the queue.

When event.wait raises BaseException, an event that was not set is removed from the queue; if it was already set and another waiter remains, the next queued event is popped and set to pass on the notification. The original exception is then re-raised.

After awaiting the event, both normal completion and errors run a finally clause that reacquires the condition under a shielded cancel scope. Thus cancellation during the registered wait does not allow it to finish without restoring the lock; acquire also updates the recorded owner.

material_error_examples: A task retains the underlying condition lock while waiting for notification.
Cancelling an already-notified waiter always consumes its notification without waking a replacement.
notify(n) wakes the newest registered waiters first.
Cancellation skips lock reacquisition and immediately escapes from the wait.

excluded_topics_avoided: Running blocking functions on worker threads
TLS EOF translation and shutdown cleanup
novelty.distinct_mechanism: Condition waiter registration, notification transfer and lock restoration under interruption. The central mechanism is condition synchronization, not defining cancellation regions or opening task groups.

questions.question: When retrieving typed extra attributes from an AnyIO file stream, how are the underlying file object, path, and file number made available? Explain the exact conditions for including the optional attributes, whether their values are captured or obtained through getters, what happens for an absent attribute with and without a supplied default, and whether that default also hides failures while constructing the attribute mapping or invoking a getter.

criteria.description: The file object attribute is always in the mapping and its getter returns the wrapped file. The path attribute is included only when the wrapped object has a name attribute; its getter constructs Path from the current file.name rather than storing a precomputed path.

Building the mapping probes file.fileno(); UnsupportedOperation causes the file-number attribute to be omitted, otherwise its getter calls fileno again when retrieved. Other probe exceptions are not caught by the file-stream mapping builder.

TypedAttributeProvider.extra indexes the attribute-to-getter mapping. A KeyError from that lookup returns an explicitly supplied default, including None; with no default it raises TypedAttributeLookupError. Exception-chain suppression is optional supporting detail.

The default is not a general exception fallback: getter execution is outside the KeyError handler, so getter failures propagate. Building extra_attributes occurs inside the try but only KeyError is handled there; non-KeyError mapping-construction errors, such as ValueError from probing a closed file, also propagate.

material_error_examples: Every file stream advertises a path and file number even for in-memory files.
The file number is probed once and that integer is permanently captured in the mapping.
Supplying a default suppresses all mapping-construction and getter exceptions.
An absent attribute without a default raises ordinary KeyError.

TLS EOF translation and shutdown cleanup
novelty.distinct_mechanism: File-backed optional attribute discovery and the boundary between missing-attribute fallback and getter/probe errors; distinct from the excluded precedence of two stapled-stream attribute mappings.

questions.question: For AnyIO RunVar, what determines whether two tasks see the same stored value, including what identifies the scope on asyncio and Trio? Explain the precedence of a stored value, a get() fallback, and the variable default; what happens if all are absent; and how set()/reset() tokens restore an unset or previously set value, including context-manager use and invalid-token errors.

criteria.description: RunVar storage is keyed by the current native event-loop token, not by task context, so tasks in one running loop share the variable value. current_token obtains that native token from the backend: the running loop on asyncio and current_trio_token on Trio.
get first returns a stored value; if absent it prefers the supplied get default over the RunVar constructor default, and raises LookupError when neither exists.

set stores the new value and returns a token containing the previous stored value or the unset sentinel. reset restores that value or deletes the entry for a previously unset variable; exiting the token context manager invokes reset.
reset rejects a token belonging to another RunVar and an already redeemed token with ValueError; a successful reset marks the token redeemed.

The constructor default overrides an explicit get() fallback.
A reset token may be reused repeatedly to restore the same value.
Resetting a token whose previous state was unset stores None.

questions.question: How does anyio.itertools.tee let its returned asynchronous iterators advance at different speeds without consuming each source item repeatedly? Explain accepted inputs and count validation, lazy shared buffering and concurrent source access, what happens when tee is applied to one of its own partially consumed iterators, and how exhaustion reaches each sibling independently.

criteria.description: tee accepts synchronous or asynchronous iterables, adapting a synchronous iterator and reusing an AsyncIterator where possible. n is normalized with operator.index; a negative count raises ValueError, and zero returns an empty tuple without constructing an iterator over the input.

Construction creates a shared state and initial unfilled link rather than consuming the source. Each iterator has its own link cursor; fetching a nonterminal link creates the next link, and returning its value advances only that iterator, allowing lagging siblings to reuse stored values.

Shared-state fill checks whether a link is filled both before and after acquiring its lock, preventing simultaneous siblings from fetching the same position twice. Constructing from an existing tee iterator shares its state and current link, so nested tee starts at that iterator's current position without advancing it or rebuilding from the original source.

Source exhaustion is stored as a filled terminal link using the end sentinel, with no successor. Each sibling raises StopAsyncIteration when its own cursor reaches that link; a faster sibling reaching it does not discard earlier values still needed by slower siblings.

material_error_examples: tee eagerly exhausts its input into a list at construction.
Each sibling has its own independent underlying iterator.
Applying tee to an existing tee iterator restarts at the beginning.
The first sibling to reach EOF immediately exhausts all other siblings.

TLS EOF translation and shutdown cleanup
novelty.distinct_mechanism: Lazy fan-out of iterable values through shared linked cursors and serialized source advancement; no stream endpoint lifecycle or byte buffering is involved.

Explain how a callback returning NotImplemented affects equality and generated inequality, and when missing ordering methods are completed or a missing equality callback causes a construction error.

When require_same_type is enabled, it checks identity of the wrapped values' classes, not wrapper-class identity or isinstance compatibility; failed requirements return NotImplemented before invoking the callback, and require_same_type=False omits this requirement.
Providing eq also installs __ne__; generated inequality calls equality and preserves NotImplemented, otherwise negating the equality result.

With one through three supplied ordering callbacks, cmp_using requires eq and raises ValueError without it; otherwise total_ordering fills the missing methods. With zero or all four ordering callbacks, this completion/error branch is not entered.

questions.question: With validation enabled, how does attrs' built-in deep mapping validator check its callback configuration and process a mapping? Explain the top-level, key, and value callback order and arguments, whether it requires a concrete dict or replaces entries with callback return values, and where processing stops when a callback raises.

The optional mapping validator first receives the instance, the field Attribute, and the whole mapping. Iteration then follows the mapping's key iteration order, calling key_validator(inst, attr, key) before value_validator(inst, attr, value[key]) for each key; the original field Attribute is reused, not a synthetic key/value attribute.

Without a supplied mapping validator enforcing a type, the implementation performs no concrete-dict check: it relies on iteration and lookup by key. Callback return values are ignored, and the validator does not use them to replace keys, values, or the mapping.

Callback exceptions are not caught or aggregated. A mapping-validator failure prevents all entry validation; a key-validator failure prevents that key's value validation; a value-validator failure prevents subsequent entries from being processed.

Each key/value callback receives a newly constructed Attribute describing that entry.

questions.question: For an attrs-generated instance representation, how do repr=False and a callable field repr affect displayed fields, and what is displayed for an unset init=False field with ordinary formatting? Explain how a cycle back to the same instance is bounded, whether the recursion guard is shared between threads, and what happens if a custom field formatter raises before representation finishes.

criteria.description: Fields with repr=False are excluded; repr=True uses ordinary repr formatting, while a callable repr is called on the field value and its result is inserted into the field fragment.

For init=False fields the generated accessor uses getattr with NOTHING as its fallback instead of direct access. With ordinary formatting, an unset field is displayed with the sentinel representation NOTHING.

The representation guard tracks object IDs currently being represented and immediately returns the literal ellipsis string for recursive entry on the same instance. The tracking context is threading.local(), so concurrent threads do not share that active-ID set.

Formatting is wrapped in try/finally that removes the instance ID on success or failure. A custom formatter exception propagates, but does not leave that instance incorrectly marked as active for subsequent representation attempts.

The recursion guard is one process-wide set shared by all threads.

An unset init=False field always raises AttributeError during ordinary generated representation.
